text.tspan: 04 · Scoreboard UI — twelve screens, grouped by app role
Conclusion: for the audience the UI is the system, and every beat of the demo has a screen that owns it — including the governance surface (/policy) that Beat 5 cannot happen without.
Service-to-service model access through the router. Application member type.
Submits a business request: intent, cost ceiling,
data classification. Exposes classification as a
control — it is a property of the REQUEST, not a
routing preference, so it stays inside Principle IV.
Inline citations as clickable superscripts opening the
source chunk; coverage percentage in the header.
The unattributable-claims panel is ALWAYS present and
says "no unattributable claims" when empty — a panel
that only appears on failure teaches the audience it is
an error state rather than a control.
No beat of its own. T-034.
Every surface showing execution is labelled SIMULATED
on the record itself, not as a corner disclaimer.
Read routing decisions and the scoreboard. User and Application.
5-second refresh; shows the timestamp of the data,
not a spinner. A stale number that admits it is stale
ONE number dominates: percentage saved against an
all-premium baseline. Per-request tier, cost, latency
and rationale beneath it. The presenter drills a row
mid-sentence and reads the rationale aloud, so the
rationale must be a plain sentence naming the deciding
factor — not a JSON blob and not a score.
Complexity inputs, candidate tiers with per-candidate
rejection reasons, policy exclusions, outcome, rationale.
Every number on the scoreboard opens to this.
500+ alerts, virtualised list (500 DOM rows stutter on
projector hardware and the stutter reads as "this does
not scale"). Sorts default to model rank, because the
ranking IS the product. A visible seed indicator carries
Rationale plus assembled evidence. Proposing escalation
from here creates an approval, never an escalation.
One query rebuilds the whole chain. The audience picks
the interaction — unrehearsed, or it is worth nothing.
Decide on pending proposals. Cannot approve own proposals. User only.
Pending proposals with their evidence packets, and
expired proposals showing that a timeout produced
The approve control renders DISABLED with the reason
stated when the viewer is the proposer — and the API
refuses the call independently. Unauthorised navigation
is hidden; unauthorised ACTIONS are visibly blocked.
Those are different on purpose: a hidden button leaves
Beat 5. No task number: this screen does not exist in
the current task list, and Beat 5 cannot run without it.
The vendor toggle has to live in the product — doing it
in the Azure portal breaks the claim that governance is
a first-class surface. Read-mostly with a single vendor
BEAT 5: disable a vendor on 12 · Policy sets, then resubmit the IDENTICAL request on 1 · Request console. No redeploy, no
Beats 3, 4 and 5 are independent: if a lane service is unhealthy, skip its beat and never debug live.
No screen — it is a shell
EVERY data view implements all five states
The empty state nobody built is the one that renders during the live run.
it and how to trigger it.
hides its own failure is one
Carries a wow moment. These three screens are the demo.
Human-in-the-loop. A person, holding a distinct identity, decides.
Evidence and audit surface — drillable to the record behind it.
Supporting screen. Still drillable; nothing on screen is decorative.
Required by a beat but NOT in the task list. Build it or lose Beat 5.
The audience reads this from ten feet away: every screen has one number that is deliberately the largest thing on it.
Nothing may look rehearsed — no pre-baked screenshots, no seeded animations. If a value is on screen it came from the API just now.
Every claim is drillable: a number a presenter cannot open is a number the audience assumes is decorative.
Polling at 5s with refetchOnWindowFocus disabled, so a presenter alt-tabbing does not trigger a visible refetch mid-sentence.
Types are generated from contracts/*.md, never hand-written, because hand-written types drift and the drift surfaces during a demo.
